```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

## What the function does

`slope_design_sensitivity()` evaluates how a declared design and covariance
model divide fitted slope information into direct and model-assisted sources.
It accepts the random-effects design matrices `Z`, planned random-effects
covariance `G`, and residual covariance matrices `R` directly.

It does **not** estimate Question-1 power for arbitrary designs. Power depends
on a separately validated testing procedure, participant count, fitting
behavior, and boundary calibration.

## Analytic sanity check

The formal two-observation Construction B gives an exact
`.80 = .20 + .60` decomposition. This is a compact cross-check connecting the
general matrix identity, its random-intercept/random-slope specialization, and
the figure value.

```{r analytic-check}
library(slopeaudit)

Z_check <- matrix(c(1, -0.5, 1, 0.5), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
colnames(Z_check) <- c("intercept", "time")
G_check <- matrix(
  c(18, sqrt(15), sqrt(15), 1),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(colnames(Z_check), colnames(Z_check))
)
check_target <- list(
  basis_type = "linear",
  outcome_units = "outcome units",
  time_or_exposure_scale = "1 time unit",
  origin_or_reference = "centered time 0",
  reference_window = "two planned observations",
  estimand = "participant-specific linear change per time unit"
)

analytic_check <- slope_design_sensitivity(
  Z = list(construction_B = Z_check),
  G = G_check,
  R = diag(2),
  target = "time",
  target_metadata = check_target
)
analytic_check$design_table[c("R_direct", "D_slope2", "Delta_fit")]
```

The result is exactly `R_direct = .20`, `D_slope2 = .80`, and
`Delta_fit = .60` up to floating-point tolerance.

## Compare four schedules on one physical scale

The following example expresses time in years, including the daily schedules.
The planned slope variance is therefore an annual-slope variance. The example
holds the covariance assumptions fixed so that only the schedules change.

```{r inputs}
make_Z <- function(time_in_years) {
  cbind(
    intercept = 1,
    time = time_in_years - mean(time_in_years)
  )
}

Z <- list(
  three_waves_two_years = make_Z(c(0, 1, 2)),
  five_waves_five_years = make_Z(seq(0, 5, length.out = 5)),
  ten_daily = make_Z((0:9) / 365),
  thirty_day_EMA = make_Z((0:29) / 365)
)

slope_variance <- 0.01
intercept_variance <- 0.5
intercept_slope_correlation <- 0.5
intercept_slope_covariance <- intercept_slope_correlation *
  sqrt(intercept_variance * slope_variance)

G <- matrix(
  c(
    intercept_variance, intercept_slope_covariance,
    intercept_slope_covariance, slope_variance
  ),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("intercept", "time"), c("intercept", "time"))
)

R <- lapply(Z, function(z) diag(1, nrow(z)))

annual_target <- list(
  basis_type = "linear",
  outcome_units = "standardized outcome units",
  time_or_exposure_scale = "1 year",
  origin_or_reference = "schedule midpoint",
  reference_window = "design-specific planned follow-up window",
  estimand = "participant-specific linear change per year"
)
```

```{r run}
design <- slope_design_sensitivity(
  Z = Z,
  G = G,
  R = R,
  target = "time",
  target_metadata = annual_target
)

comparison <- design$design_table[
  c("design_id", "R_direct", "D_slope2", "Delta_fit")
]
comparison[-1] <- lapply(comparison[-1], round, digits = 4)
comparison
```

The expected values are:

| Design | `R_direct` | `D_slope2` | `Delta_fit` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 waves / 2 years | 0.0196 | 0.1642 | 0.1446 |
| 5 waves / 5 years | 0.1351 | 0.2720 | 0.1369 |
| 10 consecutive days | 0.000006 | 0.2083 | 0.2083 |
| 30-day EMA | 0.000169 | 0.2345 | 0.2343 |

The daily schedules are dense but short when the target is an annual slope.
Their fitted determinacy comes almost entirely from the joint covariance
model. More measurements do not automatically create a strong direct slope
contrast; temporal span and residual structure matter.

## Residual-correlation sensitivity

Independent residuals are the primary public example. If a separately fitted
and scientifically justified model supplies an AR(1)-like covariance, pass it
as `R` and label the result as a matrix sensitivity, not as an `lme4` fit.

```{r ar1}
ar1_covariance <- function(n, rho, variance = 1) {
  index <- seq_len(n)
  variance * rho ^ abs(outer(index, index, "-"))
}

R_ar1 <- Map(
  function(z) ar1_covariance(nrow(z), rho = 0.5),
  Z
)

design_ar1 <- slope_design_sensitivity(
  Z = Z,
  G = G,
  R = R_ar1,
  target = "time",
  target_metadata = annual_target
)

merge(
  design$design_table[c("design_id", "R_direct")],
  design_ar1$design_table[c("design_id", "R_direct")],
  by = "design_id",
  suffixes = c("_independent", "_AR1_sensitivity")
)
```

## Connection to the validated Question 1 power cells

The Question 1 bootstrap validation study separately validated the production Question-1 test for 100
participants, slope variance `.01`, residual variance `1`, and the 3-wave and
5-wave schedules above. The completed support rates were 0.064 and 0.181 when
the intercept-slope correlation was 0, and 0.085 and 0.414 when it was 0.5.
Those are empirical results from the completed nested simulation, not values
returned by `slope_design_sensitivity()`.

The matrix calculation describes information sources under supplied
assumptions; power requires a separately specified testing procedure.
